questions.question: What is a near miss?
choices: Patient harm caused by treatment
An error or unsafe event that could have caused harm but did not reach the patient or did not cause injury
A routine patient complaint
A result reviewed on time
questions.explanation: Near misses reveal system vulnerabilities before a patient is harmed and should support learning and prevention.

questions.question: What is the first priority when a possible clinical error is identified?
choices: Determine who is at fault
Protect and assess the patient, stop/correct the unsafe action, and escalate as needed
Complete the event report before assessing the patient
Delete the relevant documentation
questions.explanation: Patient safety comes first. Investigation and reporting follow urgent assessment, mitigation, stabilization, and escalation.

questions.question: How does an event report differ from clinical documentation?
choices: They are interchangeable
Clinical documentation records patient care and communication; an event report is a separate internal safety-learning process
Only the event report is needed after harm
Clinical documentation should be removed after reporting
questions.explanation: The record must accurately describe clinical facts, assessment, treatment, and communication. Event reports have a separate role under institutional policy.

questions.question: Which is an example of an unsafe condition?
choices: A named backup clinician reviews critical results during absences
An unassigned inbox for significant test results
A patient receiving clear return precautions
A pharmacist confirming a high-risk medication change
questions.explanation: Unclear result ownership creates a foreseeable risk that important information will not be reviewed or acted on.

questions.question: What does a just-culture approach seek to do?
choices: Punish every error identically
Ignore unsafe conduct
Distinguish human error, at-risk behavior, and reckless behavior while improving the system
Prevent staff from reporting near misses
questions.explanation: Just culture supports learning and fair accountability. It examines system contributors while responding appropriately to different types of behavior.

questions.question: A critical imaging result was missed because the assigned clinician was on leave. What is the best systems response after patient follow-up is addressed?
choices: Assume the absence was the only cause
Create reliable coverage, ownership, escalation, and tracking for significant results
Stop ordering imaging
Send every result to every clinician
questions.explanation: A safer system does not depend on one person being available. Clear coverage and escalation reduce recurrence.

questions.question: Why should a clinic analyze a corrected wrong-specialty referral?
choices: No action is needed because no harm occurred
The near miss may reveal workflow or order-design vulnerabilities that could harm a future patient
It proves the clinician is incompetent
It replaces verifying the correct referral
questions.explanation: Near misses are an opportunity to improve the process before patient harm occurs. The correct referral still must be confirmed.

questions.question: Which safeguard is most useful for reducing communication omission during a handoff?
choices: A vague statement that the patient is stable
Structured communication that includes severity, pending issues, uncertainty, and next action
Removing all questions from the handoff
Assuming the EHR note is enough
questions.explanation: Structured handoff tools make critical content more reliable and help transfer responsibility, uncertainty, and contingency planning.

questions.question: What is a balancing measure in a quality-improvement project for result alerts?
choices: Whether the change creates excessive nonactionable alerts or delays other work
Whether the project has a title
Whether one staff member likes the software
Whether the patient has a portal account
questions.explanation: Balancing measures identify unintended harm. Too many low-value alerts can create alert fatigue and reduce safety.

questions.question: A patient has dizziness after unknowingly taking duplicate similar medications from two prescribers. What is the best immediate FNP reasoning?
choices: Treat it as a clerical issue only
Assess stability and exposure, reconcile actual use, coordinate with pharmacy/prescribers, and create one clear plan
Ask the patient to choose one bottle at random
Wait until the next annual visit
questions.explanation: Duplicate medication exposure may create acute harm. It requires patient assessment and mitigation as well as system learning.
